properties.description: Free-text elaboration of a transferability fact the controlled vocabularies can't capture. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment` on whatever it is attached to.

The validity envelope, as role/dimension/value statements. Required, but **an empty array is a meaningful value**, the same way it is for `rules`: it says the results were assessed and carry no validity boundary. An earlier draft required at least one entry, on the reasoning that inventing a boundary to satisfy the schema is worse than leaving a workflow unmodelled. That is still true, and the minimum did not achieve it: it made "valid everywhere" inexpressible except by drawing a world-sized polygon, and it gave a source that states no boundary no honest representation at all, rather than one saying exactly that. Say which case it is in `transferabilityNotes`.

Identifier for this constraint, so a rule can cite it in `when[].constraint`. Optional only for a constraint no rule refers to.
An **IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name** (see bblocks://ogc.ogc-utils.iri-or-curie). A local name is resolved against the document's base URI and is right for a constraint specific to one workflow. An IRI or CURIE gives the constraint a **global identity**, which is what makes a boundary shareable: the EURO-CORDEX EUR-11 domain is the same extent for several FOCAL workflows, and each restating it as a private local name leaves nothing able to tell that they are the same boundary. Declaring it here under its global identifier says so.
A CURIE expands only if its prefix is declared in the JSON-LD context (via `x-jsonld-prefixes` or an imported block); an undeclared prefix is read as a URI scheme and `acme:eur11` stays `acme:eur11`, which validates and means nothing. Use a full IRI unless the prefix is known to be in scope.
Giving a constraint a global identifier makes the boundary shareable, not fetchable: it is still declared in full in every statement that cites it, so a reader always has the extent in front of them. What the identifier buys is being able to ask which workflows are bounded by this exact domain.
Which aspect of the envelope this statement describes. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.

Which axis of variation this statement constrains, and therefore what shape `value` takes. Open vocabulary, seeded from the eight FOCAL pilot questionnaires and expected to grow; a new term needs no schema change unless it also needs a new `value` shape.

Why this value is what it is, where that is not self-evident: an approximated geometry, a fact inferred rather than stated by the source, a granularity the source left open. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment`. Mixed in from bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.notes.

JSON Pointer (RFC 6901), or several, to the input of the annotated document that this condition is **tested against**: what the user gives, such as the area of interest or the selected species (e.g. `/inputs/species`). Several pointers are for one fact spread over several inputs, such as latitude and longitude.
Not the same as an artifact's `artifactRef`, although the mechanism is the same. `artifactRef` says that an input *is* the thing a rule would replace; `inputRef` says that the condition is checked against what is given there. The two often differ: a species constraint is tested against the species selection and governs a trait table.
Optional. A consumer such as a questionnaire UI composes its wording from the referenced input's own label and description and from the structured `value`.

The constraint value, shaped by `dimension`:
- `spatial`/`jurisdictional` — a geometry, as `{"asWKT": "POLYGON((...))"}`. WKT rather
  than GeoJSON coordinate arrays: it uplifts to a real `geo:wktLiteral`, which is the
  form GeoSPARQL's topological functions actually operate on, it is one value rather than
  a nested array so nothing is lost or reshaped in uplift, and it is dramatically more
  compact (UP-WF2's European coverage MultiPolygon costs a few hundred characters
  instead of 1,283 lines of Turtle). An approximate extent is expected and fine — a
  published bounding box for a model domain, say — but it must be a real extent, since a
  free-text place name cannot answer the containment question this dimension exists for.
- `temporal` — either `{"startDate", "endDate"}` (a calendar span, uplifting to
  `dcat:startDate`/`dcat:endDate` on a `dcterms:PeriodOfTime`) or `{"scenarioMarker"}`
  for results that are not calendar-indexed at all. A Global Warming Level is the
  evidenced case: it is reached in different years under different emissions scenarios
  and ensemble members, so a calendar interval would be a fabrication rather than a
  simplification. Markers are concepts, not free text, so `GWL+1.5` written two ways by
  two pilots is one thing rather than two.
- `grid-structure` — the set of grid types the workflow's gridded inputs may be on, as
  `{"gridTypes": ["regular-latlon", "rotated-pole"]}`. A whitelist rather than a
  description: `inside` means the target data's grid is one of these, `outside` that it
  is not. This is a structured branch and not prose because UP-WF3's constraint ("other
  projections are not handled") is a hard interface requirement over a small enumerable
  set — mechanically checkable, and *more* so than a bounding box, since the terms carry
  the CF-conventions `grid_mapping_name` as their `skos:notation` and the datasets in
  question declare exactly that.
- **value ranges** — `{"variables": [{"name", "unit", "min", "max"}], "statistic"}`:
  the values of named variables within which the claim holds, such as the training domain
  of a model (`input-domain`) or the indicator limits of a classification (`climatic`).
  `inside` means every listed variable is within its range. Usually the variables are
  derived from the inputs, so the condition cannot be settled before running; a consumer
  reports it as unknown, never as satisfied.
- **any dimension, as an analogy** — `{"scheme": ..., "sameClassAs": ...}`, saying the
  target must fall in the same class of a published classification as some reference
  does. This is the shape of every "comparable to where we calibrated" claim in the
  corpus, and it is a *relation*, not a value: the source says the target must resemble
  the training area, and says nothing about which classes the training area is in.
  Enumerating those classes would state something the source never said and would go
  stale the moment the training geometry is corrected, so the default is to name the
  reference and let a platform derive the rest. Tested with `same-class-as` /
  `different-class-from` rather than `inside`/`outside`.
- `ecological`/`climatic`/anything else — a plain string, where no classification
  captures the claim. "A comparable ecological range" does not become machine-checkable
  by being wrapped in coordinates it does not have. A rule may still cite such a
  constraint; the condition is then a judgement a person makes, stated in the same
  structure, which is honest about where automation stops. Prefer the analogy shape above
  where a scheme does capture it: it says the same thing and a machine can settle it.

The extent as a WKT literal, uplifting to `geo:asWKT` with datatype `geo:wktLiteral`. An optional leading CRS URI is permitted, per GeoSPARQL; without one, CRS84 (longitude/latitude in degrees) is assumed, as GeoSPARQL specifies.

Start of the period, as an ISO 8601 year, year-month, or date. Granularity is workflow-specific and deliberately not fixed, but the format is, so two periods stated at the same granularity compare correctly as plain string ordering.
End of the period, in the same form as `startDate`.
A non-calendar, scenario-indexed temporal position, as a concept from the FOCAL scenario-markers scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). Open: other scenario indices may follow.

properties.title: Grid structure (set of accepted grid types)

properties.description: The grid types the workflow accepts, as concepts from the FOCAL grid-types scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). The whole array is the constraint: a target is `inside` it if its grid is one of these. Open vocabulary, seeded only with the two terms UP-WF3 evidences and cross-walked to CF-conventions `grid_mapping_name` values, so adding a projection is a lookup in the CF table rather than a judgement.
The variable, by the name the workflow uses.
Unit of `min` and `max`, as a plain string. Not a QUDT IRI, unlike acceptance criteria: derived variables carry units such as `z-score` or a national coding that have none.
Lowest value inside the range. Omit for an open lower end.
Highest value inside the range. Omit for an open upper end.

How the target's values are aggregated before they are compared, e.g. `multi-year mean`. Omit when each value is compared as it is. How the bounds themselves were derived (percentiles of training data, say) belongs in `transferabilityNotes`.

The published classification system this constraint is evaluated in, as a concept from the FOCAL classification-schemes vocabulary (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). FOCAL names the scheme and records where its terms live; it does not restate them, the same discipline applied to QUDT units and CF grid mappings.

The reference whose classification the target must share, normally the `id` of another constraint in the same envelope — typically the `trained-on` extent. **This is the preferred form**, and the only one usable with a scheme that publishes no term identifiers: nothing has to name a class, so a platform classifies the reference geometry and the target and compares. It also stays correct when the reference geometry is replaced by a better one, which an enumerated class list would not.

Explicitly stated classes, as an alternative to naming a reference. Use only where the source actually states them: deriving them from a reference and writing them here turns an inference into an assertion. Cite the scheme's own identifiers — EUNIS habitats are published by the EEA, and Koppen-Geiger classes are published by FOCAL itself (`.../koppen-geiger/Cfb`) precisely because no maintainer publishes them. Each classification-schemes concept records where its terms live.

`true` says outright that the source named no validity boundary and no adaptation step, which is what an empty `envelope` and an empty `rules` mean but do not announce: a reader cannot tell those two empty arrays from a form nobody filled in. It records what the source said, not a finding that anyone assessed the results, and it is not a verified claim; say who made it in `transferabilityNotes`. Only meaningful, and only valid, alongside an empty `envelope` and an empty `rules`; omit it otherwise. Not evidenced by any pilot workflow today; see the illustrative example.

Whether the thing this statement describes needs training or calibration data to be re-created somewhere else. `false` is a positive statement of the source ("does not require ML training", "Nil"), not an absence: omitting the property says nobody has said. `true` says a model is fitted to data, which is what `retrain` actions and `trained-on` envelope entries presuppose. `false` alongside a `trained-on` envelope entry is contradictory and is rejected by the shapes. Evidenced by every questionnaire that answers question 5: two say yes (FP-WF1, FP-WF3) and six say no (FP-WF2, FP-WF4, FP-WF5, UP-WF1, UP-WF2, UP-WF3).
The reference and calibration artifacts this statement's rules govern, each declared once and cited by `rules[].appliesTo`. May be empty when every rule is about the workflow as a whole.

Identifier for this artifact, cited by `rules[].appliesTo`. An IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name resolved against the document base (see bblocks://ogc.ogc-utils.iri-or-curie). A shared reference dataset that several workflows depend on is worth identifying globally, for the same reason a shared envelope constraint is.
Label identifying the artifact, in the words the source used (e.g. "downscaled FOCAL climate data", "Quitt climate-zone thresholds/limits"). Uplifts to `dcterms:title` on a `prov:Entity`.

What kind of thing this artifact is, independent of whether an executable workflow description exists that could give it an identifier yet. The eight FOCAL questionnaires' artifacts are not uniformly workflow inputs: some are inputs, some are outputs later reused as another run's input (a trained model), and some never appear in an executable graph at all (physical infrastructure to be re-deployed; an optional validation reference). Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.

What a dataset must satisfy to serve as this artifact: the variable it must carry, the units that variable may be in, the axes it must have, the grids it may be on, any schema it must conform to. See bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.acceptanceCriteria.
**This is what makes a `replace-with-local-equivalent` rule actionable.** The action says something must change; these say what would count as having changed it correctly, which is what a platform needs in order to accept or reject a candidate dataset on the user's behalf rather than hand the question back to a person.
It lives on the artifact rather than on the rule because it is a standing property of the interface, true whether or not anything is being transferred. A substitution is merely when it becomes visible. Optional, and thinly evidenced (UP-WF3, and UP-WF2's raster conventions) because the questionnaires never asked.

The variables the data must carry. **Conjunctive**: every entry must be satisfied. A single threshold value is one entry with only `units`.
The STAC datacube extension describes what a dataset contains; this states what a replacement must provide. The two correspond only partly.
The name the workflow expects the variable to be called. A plain string: a standard name says what a quantity is, this says what the code looks for.

Instead of `name`: the variable must be called what the artifact currently in use calls it. For sources that state the requirement as that relation and never give a name; guessing a literal would assert something they did not say.

CF standard name of the quantity. Says what a name cannot, such as net against downwelling radiation. A list is **an OR-set**: any one is acceptable, e.g. a quantity accepted either as a flux or as an accumulation. Give it only where the quantity is certain.
Units the variable may be in, as QUDT unit IRIs (relative names resolve against `http://qudt.org/vocab/unit/`). **An OR-set:** any one is acceptable.

Axes the data must have, as concepts from the FOCAL axes scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). **Conjunctive**, unlike `units` and `gridTypes`: every axis listed must be present. UP-WF3 requires a time axis, without which its rolling accumulation has nothing to accumulate over.

The grids the data may be on, from the same open scheme an envelope constraint's `grid-structure` dimension uses. **An OR-set.**
Not a duplicate of that dimension: the two do different jobs. An envelope constraint is a boundary a *rule is conditioned on* — cite it in `when` and the rule fires when the target falls outside it. These criteria are a specification a *candidate is checked against* once the rule has already fired and says to substitute something. State the constraint at the envelope when it bounds the workflow as a whole, and here when it binds this one artifact; UP-WF3 happens to be a case where both readings are available, because its only gridded input is also the whole of its gridded interface.

properties.title: Time axis requirements
properties.description: What the data's time axis must look like. Not the envelope's `temporal` dimension, which says for which period results hold.
Required time step, as an ISO 8601 duration (`dcat:temporalResolution`).
CF `calendar` values accepted as they are. An OR-set. Say in `transferabilityNotes` what happens to the others, where the source does.
Years of data needed **before** the requested period, e.g. 30 for a reference history.
`true`: no gaps are allowed in the required data.
Start of the span the data must cover, as an ISO 8601 year, year-month or date (`dcat:startDate`). A requirement on the data, not the period for which results hold.
End of the span the data must cover (`dcat:endDate`). Optional; omit it where the source states only a start.

Schemas or specifications the data must conform to, as identifiers. Uplifts to `dcterms:conformsTo`, the term catalogues already use for exactly this.
No current record uses it. It was drafted for UP-WF2's planned Heat Risk Indicator (census data "preferably following a schema compatible with Eurostat's"), which the owners say is not part of the workflow today. Where a preference is genuinely soft, `transferabilityNotes` is the honest home for it.

A requirement that does not reduce to the properties above, or a qualification on one that does. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment`. Mixed in from bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.notes. Not a criterion on its own: a criteria object needs at least one structured property.

JSON Pointer (RFC 6901), or several, into the document this statement annotates. For the CWL profile in bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.workflow that means `/inputs/<id>` or `/outputs/<id>`, but the pointer carries no CWL assumption.
For a `workflow-input` or `workflow-output` artifact it locates the artifact itself: what a rule would replace. For an `infrastructure` artifact, such as a data cube, it locates the inputs **through which the service is given** (connection, registry); replacing the service means pointing those inputs at another one. An `external-resource` has nothing in the document to point at.
Optional, and only fillable once the inputs are declared. Omit it rather than guess.
Free-text note about the artifact. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment`.

What must happen, to which artifacts, under which conditions. **An empty array is a meaningful value**: it says the artifacts were assessed and none needs adapting, which is a positive portability fact and quite different from the property being absent, which says nobody has looked. Requiring at least one entry would force anyone in the first situation to invent a rule.

Identifiers of the artifacts this rule governs, from the enclosing statement's `artifacts`. Several artifacts may share one rule — FP-WF2's forest-type service and species composition table do, both bounded by the same map. Not every artifact bounded by one subject belongs in the same rule, though: FP-WF2's two species trait tables cover different species, so each has its own constraint and rule. Omit `appliesTo` for a rule that applies to the workflow as a whole.
The conditions under which this rule fires, ANDed together. Two conditions here mean both must hold; two rules mean either suffices.

The `id` of an envelope constraint in the enclosing statement's `envelope`, written the same way it is declared there — an IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name. Whichever form is used, the constraint must still be declared in the statement, so a reader has the extent in front of them rather than a bare identifier: a global identifier makes a boundary shareable, it does not make it fetchable.

How the target is compared against that constraint. `outside` is the condition under which almost every evidenced FOCAL rule fires; `inside` states the complementary case, which is what lets a cascade be written without losing its connecting condition — UP-WF2's "reuse within the domain, otherwise substitute or fail" is two rules over the same constraint. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab, where each term also records how it is evaluated per dimension.
A coarse statement of what fires this rule, for cases where no envelope constraint can be cited precisely. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.

JSON Pointers (RFC 6901) to the parts of the annotated document this rule's outcome bears on — for the CWL profile in bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.workflow, typically `/steps/<id>` or `/outputs/<id>`, though the pointer carries no CWL assumption.
**This is what `component-not-executable` needs to be actionable.** Without it the action names no component, so "hot-spot characterization cannot run" and "the workflow cannot run" are the same statement, and per-artifact answers cannot be assembled into the per-workflow verdict (*runs as is* / *runs in part* / *cannot run here*) that a deployment platform actually has to produce. UP-WF2 is the evidenced case: losing CLMS costs it one step, not the run.
Optional, and meaningful for any action: a `replace-with-local-equivalent` rule may equally name the outputs whose quality changes. Omit it rather than guess, the same way `artifactRef` is omitted where no real Application Package exists to point into.
One or more actions, any of which resolves the rule — an OR-set, not a required combination. No evidenced case needs two applied simultaneously.

Whether applying one of `actions` is mandatory once the conditions hold. Defaults to true. When false, skipping is allowed but degrades result quality or trust rather than blocking execution — say what degrades in `transferabilityNotes`.
This is about validity, not executability. Whether the workflow can run without an input at all is the workflow description's to say (in CWL an optional input is `File?`, with a step `when`). `mandatory` says whether, once the target is outside the artifact's coverage, replacing it is compulsory or may be skipped at the cost of trust.
Says nothing on a rule whose only action is `reuse-as-is`: "you must do nothing" and "you may do nothing" are the same instruction. Omit it there.
Named `mandatory` rather than `required`: a data property spelled like a JSON Schema keyword reads as the keyword, and this one sits beside real `required` lists.
